subsection: 5. Autocracy in the East: Balkan nationalism (Greece and Serbia) and serfdom in Russia

notes.h: The Ottoman Empire and the Eastern Question
notes.b: In 1815 the Ottoman Empire still ruled south-eastern Europe, but its grip was weakening. The Eastern Question asked what would happen to Ottoman lands as its power declined, and which Great Power would gain from it; this question drives the whole story of Balkan nationalism.
points: The Ottoman Empire, ruled by the Sultan from Constantinople, was a Muslim state governing a largely Orthodox Christian population in the Balkans, including Greece, Serbia and the Danubian principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia.

The Sultan ruled Balkan Christians through local officials and the millet system, in which each religious community ran its own religious and civil affairs, so the Orthodox were led by the Ecumenical Patriarch in Constantinople.
The millet system gave religious communities legal autonomy but no political rights, and non-Muslims paid a poll tax (an extra tax on each person), which fed resentment of Ottoman rule.

Ottoman power was declining: central control was weak and local governors and the Janissaries (the Sultan's elite troops) often acted independently. Sultan Mahmud II (reigned 1808–39) tried to reform and destroyed the Janissary corps in 1826.

Russia claimed to protect Orthodox Christians because they shared its religion, sought passage through the Straits (the Bosporus and Dardanelles), and gained influence over Moldavia and Wallachia after its wars with the Ottomans; until 1821 these were ruled by Greek (Phanariot) princes appointed by the Sultan.

Austria feared Russian expansion into the Balkans and nationalism among its own Slavs, so it wanted the Ottoman Empire kept intact as a barrier. Britain wanted to protect its route to India, which ran through the eastern Mediterranean and the Straits, and to keep Russia out of the Mediterranean.

France had interests in the Levant (the eastern Mediterranean coast) and acted as protector of Catholics in the Holy Places. Because each Power wanted a different outcome, every Ottoman crisis became a Great Power quarrel.
notes.tip: Examiners reward explaining each Power's motive (Russia, Austria, Britain, France) rather than listing events, so learn one clear interest for each.

notes.h: Why Balkan nationalism grew
notes.b: Balkan Christians had lived under Ottoman rule for centuries without rebelling together. In the early nineteenth century several forces gave them a sense of national identity and the hope that revolt could succeed.
points: Religion and language gave a shared identity: the Orthodox Church and Greek or Serbian speech marked Christians as a people distinct from their Muslim rulers.
Ottoman misrule, such as the abuse of Serbs by the Janissary garrison, gave people a grievance that made revolt seem worth the risk.
Merchants and the diaspora (communities living abroad) supplied money, education and contacts. The Philiki Etaireia, for example, was founded by Greek merchants.
The example of the French Revolution showed that a people could claim rights and a nation, which encouraged educated Greeks and Serbs to think in national terms.
Nationalists hoped for Russian help because Russia was Orthodox and often at war with the Ottomans, although Russia in practice helped only when it suited its own interests.
Nationalism, as used here, means the belief that a people sharing religion, language and history should govern itself in its own state.
notes.tip: When asked why Balkan nationalism grew, give several causes with a reason each: religion and language, misrule, merchants, the French Revolution and the hope of Russian help.

notes.h: Serbia: the risings and autonomy, 1804–1830
notes.b: Serbia's path to autonomy was two risings, then a slow negotiated autonomy that depended on Russian pressure on the Sultan.
points: The First Serbian Uprising began in February 1804 under Karadjordje (Đorđe Petrović, 'Black George'). It was aimed against the dahije, Janissary chiefs who had seized power in the pashalik (province) of Belgrade and terrorised the Serbs.

The rising was crushed in 1813 because Russia made peace with the Ottomans in 1812 (the Treaty of Bucharest) before Napoleon's invasion, so the Serbs lost their ally. The Ottomans reconquered Serbia and Karadjordje fled across the Danube to Austrian territory.

The Second Serbian Uprising came in 1815 under Miloš Obrenović, who combined limited fighting with negotiation with the Ottoman government. This worked better than all-out war against a stronger enemy.
Russian–Ottoman agreements then bound the Sultan to grant Serbian autonomy: the Akkerman Convention (October 1826) and the Treaty of Adrianople (September 1829), which also ended a Russo-Ottoman war.
A decree (hatt-i sharif) of the Sultan in 1830 recognised Serbia as an autonomous principality with Miloš as hereditary prince, and Serbia's territory was enlarged in 1833.

Autonomy had limits. Serbia stayed under Ottoman suzerainty (the Sultan remained overlord), paid an annual tribute that was the price of its autonomy, and Ottoman garrisons stayed in Belgrade and other fortresses.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the leaders: Karadjordje led the 1804 rising and Miloš Obrenović the 1815 rising. A paragraph that confuses them loses marks.

notes.h: Serbia: rivalry and the limits of autonomy, 1830–1878
notes.b: Autonomy did not bring calm. Two families, the Obrenovićs and the Karadjordjevićs, fought for the throne, and Serbia's rulers were still checked by the Ottomans and the Great Powers.
points: Miloš ruled autocratically and rivals were removed. Karadjordje returned to Serbia in 1817 and was murdered, on Miloš's orders according to most accounts.
The liberal Sretenje Constitution of February 1835 limited Miloš's power but was suspended within weeks under pressure from Russia, Austria and the Ottomans, who disliked a liberal Serbia.

An Ottoman statute of 1838 gave power to a council of notables to limit the prince, and Miloš abdicated in 1839. His son Milan died within weeks, and his other son Mihailo ruled 1839–42 before being overthrown.
Alexander Karadjordjević, son of Karadjordje, was prince 1842–58. Miloš was restored in 1858 and died in 1860, and Mihailo's second reign (1860–68) followed.
In 1867 the Ottoman garrisons left the fortresses, a real gain in Serbian control; Mihailo was assassinated in 1868. Full independence came only in 1878, recognised at the Congress of Berlin.
In 1844 Ilija Garašanin, a Serbian minister, drew up the secret Načertanije, a plan for a larger South Slav state under Serbian leadership, which shows Serbian nationalism growing more ambitious.
Serbia's example of autonomy under a local prince influenced other Balkan nationalists, who saw that pressure plus Great Power support could win self-government.
notes.tip: Learn Serbia's dated steps as a chain: 1804, 1815, 1830, 1867, 1878. Essays on Balkan nationalism are marked on dated evidence for each stage.

notes.h: Greece: the Philiki Etaireia and the rising of 1821
notes.b: The Greek revolt began as a secret plot by Greek merchants. It failed in the north but caught fire in the Peloponnese, the southern peninsula of Greece, and soon declared itself a nation.
points: The Philiki Etaireia (Friendly Society) was a secret society founded in Odessa in 1814 by Greek merchants. It planned an armed rising against the Ottomans, recruited among merchants and intellectuals, and hoped for Russian support.

Alexander Ypsilantis, a Greek officer in the Russian army, crossed into Moldavia in March 1821 to launch a rising in the Danubian principalities. Tsar Alexander I disowned him, so he received no Russian help.

The Ottomans defeated Ypsilantis at Dragashani in June 1821, so the rising in the principalities failed. Name only Alexander, not his brother Demetrios, who fought in the Peloponnese, so that the two are not confused.
The rising in the Peloponnese began in March 1821 (25 March is celebrated as Greek Independence Day) and spread to central Greece and the islands.

Atrocities occurred on both sides, for example at Tripolitsa. When the Greeks took Tripolitsa, the Ottoman centre in the Peloponnese, in September 1821 they massacred its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants.
The Ottomans took reprisals: Patriarch Gregory V was hanged in Constantinople on Easter Sunday in April 1821, and in 1822 the Chios massacre killed or enslaved many thousands of Greeks.
The First National Assembly at Epidaurus declared independence in January 1822 and adopted a provisional constitution, so the rebels now claimed to be a state and not just rebels.
Civil wars among the Greek leaders in 1823–25 weakened the rising and left it open to counter-attack.
notes.tip: For paragraph questions give the sequence with dates: Philiki Etaireia 1814, the 1821 rising, Epidaurus 1822, Chios.

notes.h: Philhellenism and the Great Powers' response
notes.b: Atrocities such as Chios turned European opinion towards the Greeks, even though Europe's conservative governments disliked rebellion. This public sympathy made it harder for the Powers to leave the Greeks to the Sultan.
points: Philhellenism, European enthusiasm for Greek independence, drew on classical education (Greece as the home of ancient culture), Christian sympathy for fellow Christians, and romanticism. It brought volunteers and money to the Greek cause.
The English poet Lord Byron arrived in Greece in 1823 and joined the cause. He died of fever at Missolonghi on 19 April 1824, which made him a symbol of the cause across Europe.
Eugène Delacroix's paintings, The Massacre at Chios (1824) and Greece on the Ruins of Missolonghi (1826), gave the Greek cause a lasting image and kept public sympathy alive.
Metternich, the Austrian chancellor, opposed the Greeks because he saw them as rebels against a legitimate ruler. At the Congress of Verona in 1822 the Greek delegates were not received.
The Egyptian ruler (pasha) Muhammad Ali sent his son Ibrahim Pasha, who landed in the Peloponnese in 1825 and brought a new wave of destruction that reduced much of the region.
Missolonghi fell to the Ottomans in April 1826 after a long siege, and the Greek cause was close to defeat. The fall strengthened European sympathy instead of ending it.
notes.tip: If asked why the Powers intervened in Greece, link public sympathy (philhellenism, Byron, Delacroix) to the Powers' own interests, since Britain and Russia acted apart from Metternich.

notes.h: Intervention, Navarino and the Treaty of Adrianople, 1826–1829
notes.b: With the Greeks near defeat, Britain, France and Russia stepped in. Their intervention, not the rebels' own strength, decided the outcome, as the fleet action at Navarino shows.
points: Nicholas I became Tsar in December 1825 and was ready to act for the Greeks, because Russia wished to protect Orthodox Christians. The St Petersburg Protocol (April 1826, Britain and Russia, after Wellington's mission) began a joint approach.
The Treaty of London (July 1827), signed by Britain, France and Russia, aimed to impose an armistice on the Ottomans and Egypt and to secure Greek autonomy. Navarino was fought as a result.

The battle of Navarino took place on 20 October 1827. British, French and Russian squadrons under the British admiral Codrington destroyed the Ottoman–Egyptian fleet in Navarino Bay, in the south-west Peloponnese.
Navarino made Greek independence possible. Ibrahim's forces could no longer be supplied by sea, and a French expeditionary force landed in the Peloponnese in 1828 and Ibrahim's army withdrew.
In the Russo-Turkish War (1828–29) Russia fought the Sultan, and in the Treaty of Adrianople (September 1829) the Sultan accepted the Powers' settlement on Greece.
The Treaty of Adrianople also gave Russia the mouths of the Danube and confirmed its influence over Moldavia and Wallachia, so Russia gained as well as the Greeks.
notes.tip: Give Navarino as 20 October 1827 and name the three Powers. Do not confuse the Treaty of London (1827, intervention), the London Protocol (1830, independence) and the Convention of London (1832, Otto).

notes.h: The Greek kingdom, 1828–1864
notes.b: Independence was won on paper in 1830, but Greece was a small state whose rulers were chosen by the Great Powers. Its first governor was killed, its first king was a foreign teenager, and many Greeks lived outside its borders.
points: Ioannis Kapodistrias, a former joint foreign minister of Russia (to 1822), was elected governor of Greece in 1827 and arrived in January 1828. He was the first governor of independent Greece.
Kapodistrias was assassinated at Nafplio in October 1831 by members of the Mavromichalis family, whose leader he had imprisoned.

The London Protocol of 3 February 1830 made Greece an independent state under the guarantee (protection) of Britain, France and Russia. This differs from the 1852 protocol of the same name on the Danish succession.
By the Convention of London in May 1832, Otto, the teenage son of King Ludwig I of Bavaria, was chosen as king. He arrived at Nafplio in 1833, so both 1832 (chosen) and 1833 (arrived) are correct.
The 1832 frontier ran from the Gulf of Arta to the Gulf of Volos, which left most Greeks outside the kingdom.
Otto's rule used Bavarian regents and officials and was autocratic. The capital moved from Nafplio to Athens in 1834, and the Bavarian regency ended in 1835.

A revolt in Athens on 3 September 1843 forced Otto to grant a constitution, adopted in 1844. In the same year Ioannis Kolettis voiced the Megali Idea ('Great Idea'), the aim of uniting all Greeks in one state, which stayed the goal of Greek nationalism.
Otto was deposed in October 1862 and the Powers chose Prince William of Denmark as King George I in 1863. Britain ceded the Ionian Islands to Greece in 1864.
notes.tip: Keep Otto's dates straight: chosen 1832, arrived 1833, constitution 1844, deposed 1862. Otto of Greece is not Otto von Bismarck.

notes.h: The Crimean War, the Treaty of Paris and Romania
notes.b: The Eastern Question exploded into a Great Power war in the 1850s. Its settlement guaranteed the Ottoman Empire but also made possible the union of Moldavia and Wallachia.
points: The war grew from a dispute over the Holy Places between Catholic monks (backed by France) and Orthodox monks (backed by Russia). In 1853 Prince Menshikov's mission to Constantinople demanded a Russian protectorate over the Sultan's Orthodox subjects.

Russia occupied Moldavia and Wallachia in July 1853, the Ottomans declared war in October 1853, and the Russian navy destroyed an Ottoman squadron at Sinope in November 1853. Britain and France declared war on Russia in March 1854.

Russia withdrew from the principalities in 1854 because of Austrian pressure. The Crimean War (1853–56) is named for the Crimea, where the siege of Sevastopol lasted 1854–55 and the city fell in September 1855; Nicholas I died in March 1855 during the war.
The Treaty of Paris (March 1856) guaranteed the integrity of the Ottoman Empire, neutralised the Black Sea (no warships or naval arsenals), and made Russia cede southern Bessarabia to Moldavia.

It also placed Moldavia and Wallachia under the collective guarantee of the Powers, ending Russia's protectorate. The Hatt-i Humayun (February 1856), a decree the Powers had pressed for, promised equality to non-Muslim subjects.
The Black Sea clauses removed Russian naval power from the region for a time, so Russia was weakened, and the Russian defeat became the trigger for emancipation of the serfs.
Alexandru Ioan Cuza was elected prince of Moldavia in January 1859 and of Wallachia in February 1859. The union as Romania was recognised by the Sultan in December 1861 and proclaimed in 1862.
Cuza was deposed in 1866 and replaced by Carol of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen. Romania stayed under Ottoman suzerainty until its independence was recognised in 1878.
notes.tip: Say that Britain and France declared war in March 1854 and the Ottomans in October 1853, not that all went to war together. Date the Treaty of Paris to 1856 and do not confuse it with Adrianople (1829).

notes.h: How far Balkan nationalism threatened European stability
notes.b: Balkan nationalism threatened the peace of Europe because every rising on Ottoman land invited the Great Powers to intervene. Yet the Powers usually co-operated to contain these crises, so the threat was real but limited.
points: Threat: each rising invited Great Power intervention and rivalry, mainly Russia against Austria and Britain, which turned the Balkans into a focus of tension.
Threat: the Greek revolt split the Congress System, because Britain and Russia acted apart from Metternich, who wanted to uphold legitimate rulers.

Threat: the Russo-Ottoman wars (1828–29 and 1853) and the Crimean War, the only war between Great Powers in 1815–1854, began over the Eastern Question. Balkan crises in the 1850s and 1860s kept the Powers in tension.

Limit of the threat: the Powers usually acted together to contain crises, as in the Treaty of London (1827), the London Protocol (1830) and the Treaty of Paris (1856). They imposed small, guaranteed states with foreign kings.

Limit of the achievement: by 1871 only a small Greece was independent, Serbia and Romania were autonomous but tributary, and most Balkan Christians (Bulgarians, most Greeks, Bosnians) still lived under Ottoman rule.
The Eastern Question stayed open, and the Ottoman Empire later got the nickname the sick man of Europe, a phrase attributed to no one here.
notes.tip: For the stability essay argue both sides with examples (threat: Navarino, 1828–29, the Crimean War; containment: the London treaties and Paris), then give a verdict. Explain each Power's motive.

notes.h: Tsarist autocracy: Alexander I
notes.b: Russia was the great autocracy of the East. Its Tsar held unlimited power, and the early hopes of reform under Alexander I faded without touching serfdom.
points: Autocracy means rule by one person with unlimited authority. In Russia the Tsar had no constitution or national parliament to limit him, the nobility served the state, and the Orthodox Church supported the throne.
Alexander I (reigned 1801–25) showed early reforming promise but took little action on serfdom. Mikhail Speransky drafted reform plans in 1809 but was dismissed in 1812.
His Law on Free Cultivators (1803) let landlords free serfs, with land, by agreement. Very few landlords used it, so serfdom stayed in place.

He granted a constitution to the Kingdom of Poland in 1815 and helped found the Holy Alliance (September 1815), and after 1815 he was involved in the Congress System. He became more reactionary after 1820.
notes.tip: Define autocracy as the Tsar's unlimited power, with no constitution or national parliament. This also helps when the term appears in a question.

notes.h: The Decembrists, 1825
notes.b: The first open challenge to the Tsar came from inside the elite. Young officers influenced by western ideas rose when the succession was unclear, and its failure shaped the reign that followed.
points: The Decembrists were secret societies of young officers and nobles, influenced by western ideas after the wars of 1812–15. The Northern Society met in St Petersburg and the Southern Society, in the Ukraine, was led by Pavel Pestel.
Alexander I died in November 1825. His brother Constantine had renounced the throne, so Nicholas succeeded, and this confusion over the succession gave the plotters their chance.
On 14 December 1825 the Decembrists rose in Senate Square in St Petersburg demanding a constitution and the end of serfdom.

Nicholas I crushed the revolt by artillery the same day, so it was over within hours. Five leaders, including Pavel Pestel and Kondraty Ryleev, were hanged in July 1826, and more than a hundred were exiled to Siberia.
The revolt shaped Nicholas's rule, which was built on repression and strong censorship.
notes.tip: For a paragraph on the Decembrists give the date (14 December 1825), their demands (a constitution and the end of serfdom), the suppression, and Nicholas I's repression.

notes.h: Tsarist autocracy: Nicholas I
notes.b: Nicholas I answered the Decembrists with a system of control and strengthened the autocracy. He tried some administrative reform but would not tackle private serfdom.
points: Nicholas I (reigned 1825–55) founded the Third Section of His Majesty's Own Chancellery in 1826, a political police force to monitor opponents of the regime.
In 1833 Sergei Uvarov, the Minister of Education, proclaimed the doctrine of Orthodoxy, Autocracy and Nationality (Official Nationality) to define Russian identity and bind subjects to the throne.
The autocracy kept rigid control of the press, universities and education, and censorship was tight under Nicholas I.
Speransky's codification of the laws appeared as the Complete Collection of the Laws (1830) and the Digest of Laws (1832–33).
Pavel Kiselev, Minister of State Domains from 1837, reformed the administration of the state peasants (peasants on state land) in 1837–41, but Nicholas did not tackle private serfdom.
Nicholas was the 'gendarme of Europe': he crushed the Polish rising of 1830–31, abolished the 1815 Polish constitution, and helped Austria crush the Hungarians in 1849.
In 1849 the Petrashevsky circle was arrested and Fyodor Dostoevsky was sentenced to death, reprieved at the place of execution and sent to Siberia, which shows how far repression went.
notes.tip: Name the three tools of Nicholas I's control: the Third Section, censorship and Official Nationality. Say 'Sergei Uvarov, the Minister of Education', not 'Count'.

notes.h: Serfdom in Russia: what it was and how widespread
notes.b: Serfdom was the foundation of Russian society and the economy. It had already vanished from western Europe, so Russia stood out as backward.
points: Serfs were peasants bound to the land and to the authority of a noble owner. Landlords controlled their labour, movement and marriage, punished them, and could sell or mortgage them.
Serfs were subject to corporal punishment and the lord's courts, and could be sent into the army for long service. The estate system kept their lives under their owners' control.
In the late 1850s there were about 22–23 million privately owned serfs, about a third of the empire's population. State peasants were roughly as numerous, so most Russians were unfree.
Serfdom had gone from western Europe by then (in France from 1789; Prussia began abolishing it in 1807), so Russia's system looked old-fashioned.
notes.tip: Say 'about a third of the population' when giving the extent, and keep privately owned serfs separate from state peasants, because the 1861 edict covered only privately owned serfs.

notes.h: Serfdom: obligations and economic effects
notes.b: Serfs paid their owners with labour or money, and the system damaged the economy. Landlords had little reason to improve estates, and the serfs had none either.
points: Barshchina was labour dues, when serfs worked on the lord's land, usually about three days a week. It was most common in the fertile black-earth region of the south.
Obrok was quitrent, a payment in money or produce, and was more common in the less fertile north and centre. Household serfs (dvorovye) worked as domestic servants.

Serfdom held back agricultural productivity: landlords had little incentive to invest and serfs had little interest in improving land they did not own. Strip farming and the commune added to the problem.
It created little demand for manufactures, since peasants had little money to spend, and tied labour to the land, so a free workforce could not grow.
Possessional serfs, and peasants tied to their villages by passports, worked in Urals ironworks and other factories, which limited the growth of a free labour force.
By 1859 about two-thirds of privately owned serfs were mortgaged by their owners to state credit institutions, so many noble estates were deeply in debt.
Serf unrest brought many local disturbances under Nicholas I, and landlords feared a Pugachev-style revolt (the great rising of 1773–75).
notes.tip: Keep barshchina (labour) and obrok (payment) apart and give a fact for each. A good 30-mark paragraph gives many short, accurate facts in order: what a serf was, the extent, the dues, the economic effects, then 1861.

notes.h: Why serfdom was challenged
notes.b: By the 1850s there were moral, economic and military arguments against serfdom. The Crimean War made the case impossible to ignore, because it exposed an army and economy held back by the system.
points: Moral argument: literature such as Ivan Turgenev's A Sportsman's Sketches (1852) showed the cruelty of serf life to educated readers, which turned opinion against the system.
Economic argument: free labour would be more productive than forced labour, and noble estates were heavily mortgaged.
Military argument: the Crimean defeat showed a backward army and economy, and a serf army could not have a large trained reserve.
Serfdom was debated in secret committees under Nicholas I, but the government took no decisive action before the Crimean War exposed the weaknesses of the system.
Fear of revolt added urgency, since serf unrest was growing and landlords remembered Pugachev.
notes.tip: For the question 'why were the serfs freed' give the Crimean defeat, economic backwardness, fear of revolt and moral pressure, each with a reason.

notes.h: Alexander II's emancipation edict, 1861
notes.b: Alexander II acted after the Crimean defeat and chose to free the serfs from above, on terms the nobles could accept. The edict gave legal freedom, but at a price for the peasants.
points: Alexander II (reigned 1855–81) made emancipation a priority because of Russia's defeat in the Crimean War, which had shown the empire's backwardness. The fall of Sevastopol in September 1855 forced Russia to accept peace in 1856.
In a speech to the Moscow nobility in March 1856 he said, in paraphrase, that it was better to abolish serfdom from 'above' than to wait until it began to abolish itself from 'below'.
Preparation began with provincial noble committees from 1857, and the Editing Commissions of 1859, set up under Yakov Rostovtsev with Nikolai Milyutin a leading member, drafted the terms.
The Manifesto and Statutes were issued on 19 February 1861 (3 March in the western calendar). This was one event and not two.
The edict freed about 22–23 million privately owned serfs from personal bondage, with rights to marry, move, own property, trade and go to court.

Peasants received allotments of land, for example, but landlords kept much of the land and often the best of it. In the black-earth provinces peasants often lost a large part of land they had worked (the otrezki, 'cut-offs').
Household serfs were freed without land, so they had freedom but no way of earning a living from the land.
notes.tip: Give the date as 19 February 1861 (Old Style) and do not treat 3 March as a different event. A document question on the edict asks its purpose, to free the serfs, and what it gave or required.

notes.h: Redemption payments, the mir and temporary obligation
notes.b: Freedom was not free. Peasants had to pay for their land over decades, through a village commune that also controlled them, and until then they still owed their old lords.
points: Until redemption (buying out the land) was agreed, peasants were temporarily obligated to their former lords, paying dues in labour or obrok for the land they used.
There was a two-year transition before the statutes took full effect. Redemption became compulsory for all remaining temporarily obligated peasants from 1883.

Redemption payments worked as a loan: the state advanced about three-quarters to four-fifths of the land's price to landlords in bonds, and peasants repaid the state over 49 years at 6 per cent interest, paying the remaining part to the landlord directly.
Many historians judge the land prices too high, so peasants paid more than the land was worth and were left poor and indebted for decades.
The mir (also called the obshchina, the village commune) received the land, redistributed strips in many areas, and was collectively responsible for taxes and redemption payments.
Peasants needed the mir's permission to leave, so it kept them tied to the village and to strip farming.
Redemption payments were halved for 1906 and abolished from 1 January 1907, after the 1905 revolution.
notes.tip: Learn the terms well enough to recognise them in a document: 49 years, redemption payments, the mir, temporary obligation. Do not confuse the mir (commune) with the zemstvo (elected council).

notes.h: Results of emancipation and the reforms that followed
notes.b: Emancipation changed the legal position of the peasants but left them poor, and it left the Tsar's power untouched. Other reforms followed because a freed society needed new institutions.
points: For peasants: personal freedom and civil rights, but land hunger, debt and poverty. Troops fired on peasants at Bezdna (Kazan province) in April 1861, who believed the real emancipation was being hidden from them.
For the economy: slow agricultural improvement, because the mir kept strip farming and tied peasants to villages, but also a gradual move to wage labour and, later, a labour supply for industry.
Landlords' debts were often deducted from their compensation, and many nobles sold land in later decades.

Emancipation came from above and kept the Tsar's power intact, with no national parliament. Radical and revolutionary opposition grew in the 1860s and 1870s, and Alexander II was assassinated on 1 March 1881.
The zemstva (elected district and provincial councils) were set up in 1864, and the judicial reform of 1864 brought jury trial, independent judges and public trials.
Town dumas (town councils) followed in 1870, and a military reform under Dmitry Milyutin in 1874 shortened service.
notes.tip: Give results for peasants, the economy and autocracy as achievements against limits. Do not confuse Dmitry Milyutin (army reform) with his brother Nikolai (emancipation commissions).

notes.h: Assessment: achievements and limits
notes.b: Both halves of this subsection show change that came from above or from outside, with real gains and real limits. Examiners reward paired judgements and a clear verdict.
points: Achievement: Serbia became autonomous (1830), Greece independent (1830–32) and Romania united (1859–62), the first national states carved from the Ottoman Empire. Greece was the first state to win full independence.

Limit: success depended on Great Power intervention and rivalry, not on the nationalists' own strength, and the new states were small with imposed rulers. Most Balkan Christians were still under Ottoman rule in 1871.
Stability: a real threat in Navarino, the 1828–29 war and the Crimean War, against containment by Great Power co-operation in London (1827 and 1830) and Paris (1856).
Achievement: emancipation ended personal bondage for about a third of the population, peacefully and from above, and opened the way to further reforms.
Limit: land loss, redemption debt, the mir and continuing poverty, with the autocracy unchanged.
Views: contemporaries were disappointed because peasants expected all the land free, whereas later historians see a major but flawed reform.
Overall: Balkan nationalism created new states but fed Great Power rivalry, while emancipation was a major reform that left the peasants with real grievances.
notes.tip: Open a Balkan essay with a thesis (partial success, dependent on Great Power interests), then give dated evidence for each part, weighing each step with 'because the Powers...'.

keyTerms.definition: The problem of what would happen to the Ottoman Empire's European possessions as its power declined, and which Great Power would benefit.
European enthusiasm for the Greek cause in the 1820s, which brought volunteers, money and political pressure for intervention.
The condition of peasants bound to the land of their noble owners, who controlled their labour, movement and marriage.
The labour dues owed by Russian serfs, who worked on the lord's land for several days each week.
The payment in money or goods that Russian serfs made to their lords instead of labour dues.
The Russian village commune, which held land collectively and was responsible for redemption payments after emancipation.
The payments made by former serfs over 49 years after 1861 to repay the government's loans to landlords for the land they received.
The officers and nobles who rose in St Petersburg on 14 December 1825 demanding a constitution and the end of serfdom.
The political police set up by Nicholas I in 1826 to monitor and repress opposition to the Tsar's government.
A system of government in which a single ruler holds unlimited power, which in Russia meant the Tsar's rule without a constitution.
The belief that a people sharing language, religion and history should form their own state, which drove the Greek and Serbian risings.

factCards.definition: The uprising led by Karadjordje Petrović in 1804 against the Janissary garrison, which began the Serbian national struggle.
Miloš Obrenović led the second Serbian rising in 1815, won autonomy for Serbia and became hereditary prince.
The Friendly Society founded in Odessa in 1814 to plan an armed rising for Greek independence from the Ottomans.
The Greek revolt began in March 1821 in the Peloponnese, and the Greeks declared independence in January 1822.
The Ottoman massacre on the island of Chios in 1822 aroused European sympathy for the Greek cause.
The battle of 20 October 1827 in which British, French and Russian fleets destroyed most of the Ottoman and Egyptian fleet, making Greek independence possible.
The 1830 agreement by the Great Powers recognising Greece as an independent state with a guarantee from Britain, France and Russia.
The Bavarian prince who became the first king of independent Greece in 1832 and was forced out in 1862.
The revolt in St Petersburg by young officers and nobles demanding a constitution and the end of serfdom, which was suppressed by Nicholas I.
Count Sergei Uvarov's doctrine of Orthodoxy, Autocracy and Nationality, which defined Russian identity under Nicholas I.
Alexander II's decree freeing Russia's serfs from personal bondage, with land and redemption payments attached.
The 49 years over which former Russian serfs were required to repay the government for the land they received in 1861.
